chapter: Bands and bandleading in New Orleans
title: Leon Rapolo, Raymond Burke and starting his own Red Hot band
summary: Back from service he joins a Leon Rapolo band, meets Raymond Burke, then books jobs under his own name, plays the Wigwam and Fun Bar, joins the union and plays campaign, St. Regis and jazz club jobs.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: It helps out a little bit. So I came back from the Coast Guard and I hadn't played for about a year or two and Leonard Wiley calls me and asks me if I wanted to play with the Leon Rapolo. Now not the original Leon Rapolo. This is the Leon Rapolo that used to direct the five piece band with the baton in the beginning. Don't laugh now. This is me recording. Okay I won't laugh anymore. You're laughing at my antics, not the- No, I just heard that story so many times. So anyway, it was good that I worked with him. I met Raymond Burke. I had never known Raymond until that time. You see the band we had, he booked a job across the river to Gay Parade. He had Rene Shea on piano, Eddie Chance on drum, Tom Brown on trombone, a bass fiddle I played, maybe trombone, maybe trombone, I don't know. I say trombone, myself and Raymond Burke. It was that five men and Leon. And then we worked up a pretty good little band over there. It wasn't bad at all. But things fell off. That's the way I started to go into business. I knew all the jazz men about that time and somebody asked me if I could get them a band. I said yeah. So I started using the fellas that I had met. And I think one of the first jobs I booked was myself and Raymond, a guy named Lou Castillo on drums, and Tester Craig played the bass fiddle, Gene Hemart played the guitar. And then I started using the name of Red Heart and his Red Heart band. I was about 48, 47, sometime around that time. And I worked up a pretty good band. I played at places called the Keyhole Across the River and I played at the Gay Parade with my own band. I played at a place called the Fun Bar, Jack Store. I used to come on television and advertise regular beer and do a few pantomimes. And then after that I went over to a place called the Wigwam for about a year. I'm talking about weekend jobs now in the last 15 years, all weekend jobs. We stayed at the Wigwam almost the whole year. Boy, I worked up a good band there. It was really the same band that I had at the Jack Store's Fun Bar. I had a good front line. I had a good front line. And that's one of my best tapes. That was made in 1951. And I have a tape. The fact that you've heard it, the Fun Bar tape, it was pretty good. The rhythm could have been a little stronger, but I had a good front line. And that's one of my best tapes. That was made in 1951. And anyway, after the Wigwam, which was a pretty nice place, I figured, well what are you going to do? I went to the dives again, so I said why don't you go in the union, I said that to myself, you might play in, you keep going up the ladder a little bit you know, because I'll play in all the voice places. Some places you'll have to light a match to see who's sitting next to you. But I went in the union and about the second day I was in I played a campaign job for Sheriff Tucker. He wasn't sheriff but he was running against Clancy. And that paid real good money. I was tickled to death. I was beginning to make money then. And I used the boys I'd play with, Raymond Bug, Tom Brown, Arnold Lugganer, and Eddie Chance and myself. We didn't use the piano. And that job brought me about three or four other campaign jobs for him, sort of a ballyhoo. And then I started to book some dance work, mostly in the union it's mostly spot dance, like conventions and fraternities. I played at St. Regis. Yeah I was in the union when I played at St. Regis for a while. And it was on it's way out then. There's another place I'm closing with my good music. But I wasn't the last man to play in there. And St. Regis. I kept on spotting as this itinerary says here. I don't know what's coming next but it's just about like it is right now. Spot jobs. I played New Orleans Country Club a few times. I played one jazz club dance. It seemed to be a little different though Dick. I still got the advertising and the paper. God bless the jazz club. They did a lot for jazz now. That's all I can say. But when I used to go to the jazz club Christmas dances, bring a 50 cent present and your dues card. But the night I played, oh boy. The atmosphere was the New Orleans Athletic Club. Goody goody. And it was five dollars a couple. And naturally it had a lot of empty tables. And everybody tried to make it, the way it looked to me, I'll take that, but not everybody. But there was no write ups about the dance and the magazine the next month. And I still say if they wouldn't have put that five dollars minimum on me, if you come and bring your card and your 50 cent present. And they had like old drawers like they used to have in the... Yeah. I'd have packed it too, because I had a good band that night. And to make it worse, before we started one of the officials came up and said give us some Christmas music. I'm there grooved up and geared up to play a jazz program, and this guy give us some Christmas music.
Pour a cold water, everything. I wouldn't say it was spiteful. I wouldn't say anything like that.
